description: How territory, dynastic claims and Scottish alliances dragged England and France into a long war.
content_html:
Why Did England and France Go to War?

The Hundred Years’ War — the series of conflicts fought between England and France from 1337 to 1453 — did not begin from a single cause. It grew from decades of competing dynastic claims, disputed territories and diplomatic rivalries. Understanding why war broke out in 1337 requires looking at the interlinked pressures on both Edward III and the French Crown.

Edward III’s Claim to the French Throne

The most dramatic grievance was Edward III’s personal claim to the French throne. When the French king Charles IV died in 1328 without a male heir, Edward — as the son of Isabella of France and the grandson of Philip IV of France — argued he had the strongest dynastic claim to be the next king of France.

The French nobility rejected this argument. They invoked an ancient legal custom, the Salic law, which excluded inheritance through the female line. Instead, they crowned Philip of Valois as Philip VI. Edward initially accepted this — he paid homage to Philip for his French lands — but as relations deteriorated, he pressed his claim as a pretext for war.

Key Fact

Edward III claimed the French throne through his mother Isabella, daughter of Philip IV of France. When Charles IV died heirless in 1328, the French nobles rejected Edward’s claim and crowned Philip VI instead, planting a dynastic grievance that Edward later used to justify war.

The English Lands in France: Aquitaine

At the root of the conflict was the long-standing problem of English-held land in France. Since 1154, English kings had held territories in France, and by the fourteenth century Aquitaine in south-west France was the most important. It was extraordinarily profitable — the wine trade alone generated significant customs revenue — and English kings were determined to keep it.

But holding Aquitaine meant English kings were also feudal vassals of the French Crown for those lands — an awkward position when relations broke down. Philip VI repeatedly sought to undermine English control of Aquitaine, supporting local French lords who disputed English authority. In 1337, Philip formally confiscated Aquitaine, claiming Edward had failed in his feudal obligations. This act made war almost inevitable.

Aquitaine was not just a symbol of royal prestige — it was an economic asset. The region’s vineyards supplied a thriving wine trade with England, and the port of Bordeaux was one of the busiest in northern Europe. English merchants, traders and the Crown itself derived significant income from this commerce. Losing Aquitaine would have been a major financial as well as political blow to Edward III and his war-making capacity.

The Auld Alliance: France and Scotland

England’s strategic position was complicated by the Auld Alliance between France and Scotland. This alliance, which stretched back to 1295, meant that when England threatened France, Scotland would threaten England’s northern border — and vice versa. Edward III had already fought a war in Scotland in the 1330s to impose his preferred candidate, Edward Balliol, on the Scottish throne.

The Franco-Scottish alliance was therefore a genuine strategic threat. If Edward committed his forces to France, the Scots — backed by French support — could raid northern England. This forced Edward to maintain a military presence in the north even while fighting in France, stretching his resources considerably.

Key Fact

The Auld Alliance meant France and Scotland were mutual allies against England. While Edward III fought in France, Scotland — backed by French diplomacy and resources — could threaten England’s northern border, forcing Edward to fight on two fronts simultaneously.

Philip VI’s Role and the Confiscation of 1337

Philip VI was not a passive figure waiting to be attacked. He actively sought to weaken English power in France. He supported David II of Scotland against Edward’s preferred candidate, encouraged French lords in Aquitaine to resist English rule, and in May 1337 formally confiscated Aquitaine from Edward, declaring him a rebellious vassal.

This confiscation was the immediate trigger for the war. Edward III responded by formally declaring himself king of France in 1337 and launching a military campaign. The war that followed would last, with interruptions, until 1453 — long after Edward III himself was dead. But the causes laid down in the years before 1337 — dynastic rivalry, disputed territory, Scottish entanglement and French provocation — shaped every aspect of the conflict that followed.

Edward III’s aims were not simply to press his claim to the French throne — that may have been as much a propaganda device as a genuine ambition. His more immediate objectives were to secure Aquitaine against French encroachment, to end French support for Scotland, and to demonstrate his military prowess to the English nobility, who expected a king to lead his armies. War also offered the prospect of plunder, ransom and glory — incentives that mattered to the military class who would have to fight it.
exam_tip_html: On a “explain a cause” question about the Hundred Years’ War, avoid listing causes without developing any one of them. Pick the cause the question asks about and explain the chain of events in detail — for example, tracing how the confiscation of Aquitaine in 1337 linked to Philip VI’s broader policy and Edward III’s dynastic ambitions. On “compare interpretations” questions, remember that different historians have emphasised different causes (dynastic, economic, strategic), so you can use this lesson to discuss WHY historians’ interpretations of the war’s origins differ.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edward III claimed the French throne through his mother Isabella, but the French crowned Philip VI in 1328 using Salic law to exclude inheritance through the female line.
  • Aquitaine was England’s most valuable overseas territory; Philip VI’s formal confiscation of it in 1337 was the immediate trigger that turned rivalry into open war.
  • The Auld Alliance between France and Scotland meant Edward III faced a two-front strategic problem, forcing him to balance campaigns in France against the ever-present threat from Scotland.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Edward III's claim to the French throne.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: Edward III was the grandson of Philip IV of France through his mother Isabella [1], giving him what he claimed was the strongest dynastic right to the French throne when Charles IV died without a male heir in 1328 [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Auld Alliance between France and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: The Auld Alliance was a long-standing treaty first formalised in 1295 [1] under which France and Scotland agreed to support each other against their shared enemy England [1]. Feature 2: The alliance created a two-front strategic threat for English kings [1] — whenever England attacked France, Scotland could raid northern England, forcing Edward III to divide his military resources [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the outbreak of the Hundred Years' War in 1337.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (dynastic rivalry over the French throne, the confiscation of Aquitaine, the Franco-Scottish alliance, or Philip VI's provocations) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge, showing how this cause connected to wider context. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to conflict without a specific cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Philip VI's confiscation of Aquitaine in 1337.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth with factual support — e.g. Edward III formally declared himself king of France and launched military campaigns, triggering the war that would last until 1453. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Isabella of France to the causes of the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance both at the time (her bloodline gave Edward III his dynastic claim; her role in the deposition of Edward II shaped English politics) and in the longer term (the dynastic claim became a recurring justification for English military intervention in France throughout the war's duration). Accurate factual knowledge integrated throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes Isabella without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important cause of the Hundred Years' War was Edward III's desire to claim the French throne.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees using precise factual knowledge. Agrees: the dynastic claim gave the war its ideological justification; Edward formally adopted the title King of France in 1337; the claim shaped English war aims throughout. Disagrees: the confiscation of Aquitaine was the immediate trigger and arguably more important economically; the Auld Alliance forced England's hand strategically; Philip VI's aggression was equally provocative. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement weighing the relative importance of causes. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present but may lack full development. Developing: Describes causes without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement reached.

knowledge_checks.q: Through which relative did Edward III claim the right to the French throne?
What event in 1337 was the immediate trigger for the start of the Hundred Years' War?
options: The signing of the Auld Alliance

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ between France and Scotland, first agreed in 1295, meant England faced a military threat on its northern border whenever it campaigned in France.
Philip VI became king of France in 1328 because the French nobility used _____ law to exclude Edward III's claim through the female line.
Match each person or place to their role in the causes of the Hundred Years' War:
right: Confiscated English territory in 1337, triggering war
Edward III's mother, whose bloodline gave him his French claim
England's most profitable overseas territory, producing wine

flashcard_questions.q: Through whom did Edward III claim the French throne?
flashcard_questions.a: His mother Isabella, daughter of Philip IV of France.

flashcard_questions.q: What legal argument did France use to reject Edward III's claim in 1328?
flashcard_questions.a: Salic law, which excluded inheritance through the female line.

flashcard_questions.q: Who became king of France instead of Edward III in 1328?
What did Philip VI do in 1337 that directly triggered the Hundred Years' War?
flashcard_questions.a: He formally confiscated Aquitaine from Edward III.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Aquitaine so valuable to English kings?
flashcard_questions.a: It produced profitable wine exports and generated significant customs revenue for the Crown.
A long-standing treaty between France and Scotland, first formalised in 1295, directed against England.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Auld Alliance first formalised?
How did the Auld Alliance create a strategic problem for Edward III?
flashcard_questions.a: Scotland could threaten England's northern border while Edward fought in France.

flashcard_questions.q: In what year did Edward III formally declare himself king of France?
The Hundred Years' War lasted from 1337 to what year?
What role did Isabella of France play in Edward III's claim to the throne?
flashcard_questions.a: She was his mother and the daughter of Philip IV, giving Edward his blood claim to France.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one practical aim Edward III had in going to war in 1337, beyond the dynastic claim.
flashcard_questions.a: To secure Aquitaine and end French support for Scotland.

glossary_terms.definition: Edward III of England, who ruled from 1327 to 1377 and launched the Hundred Years' War partly to press his claim to the French throne.
Daughter of Philip IV of France and mother of Edward III of England, whose blood gave Edward his claim to the French crown.
Philip VI of France, who became king in 1328 when the French nobility rejected Edward III's claim; his policies directly provoked the war.
The wealthy wine-producing region of south-west France held by English kings, the richest overseas possession of the English Crown.
The long-standing alliance between France and Scotland, first formalised in 1295, directed against their shared enemy England.
